newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish bond spread seen defended by fundamentals.
newsitem.headline: Spanish bond spread seen defended by fundamentals.

text.p: Solid Spanish fundamentals will cap a widening of the Spanish 10-year spread to Bunds at a maximum of 125 basis points, despite Euromarket worries over the single currency project, economists said.
"The Spanish market is very well supported (by fundamentals)," said Carmen Hernansanz, economist at Merrill Lynch in Madrid. "I believe a ceiling of 100 to 125 is reasonable (in the spread)."

Today, the Spanish 10-year spread was trading at around 75 basis points, not far above its historic low of 64 bps hit on May 21, having declined from about 330 in March, 1996 and from 500 in the summer of 1995.
Economists attribute the relatively low long-end yield spread to the unusual degree of economic stability that Spain has enjoyed in recent months.

"It's almost certain that Spain will be in the Euro's first wave, the problem is whether there will be a euro, and if so, if it will be more or less flexible," said Juan Antonio Mielgo, economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
Given the strength of domestic fundamentals, Mielgo put a ceiling for the spread at 100 basis points.
Other economists were even more optimistic than that.
"I would expect the (Spanish) spread to move from 65 to 80 basis points," a London-based economist said.
And another London analyst said the spread could widen no more than at 85 basis points.
BCH on Monday assigned Spain a 88.7 percent probability of being in EMU in 1999, according to a daily calculation based on market swaps rates. Italy was at 59.4 percent.
Chief among Spain's economic achievements is a drop in the inflation rate, a stable currency and fiscal austerity.

The consumer price rate fell to 1.7 percent in April, less than half last December's 3.2 percent. The peseta, with a rocky history of depreciations, has traded stabily and without major incident for more than two years.
Fiscal tightness and a four-point fall in the official interest rates in just 17 months have led to huge gains in Spanish debt prices and in the stock market.
In addition, Spain has not had to sacrifice its growth rates to stability. The official goal of three percent gross domestic product growth in 1997 seems ever more likely, analysts say.
Despite the sturdy backdrop, Spanish assets cannot ignore market volatility when facing external shocks as the ones recently experimented, strategists said.
The switch in French power to the left from right was one worrying factor.

In recent days, European markets have also worried that the fight between Bonn's government and the Bundesbank over the gold revaluation project could end up affecting the overall European single currency project.
"This is spoiling the credibility of the single currency project," said a daily note of Societe Generale in Madrid.
Despite these renewed EMU jitters, dealers in Madrid were optimistic that the new two fires could be extinguished quickly.
Earlier on Tuesday, remarks by Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer and from German Chancellor Helmut Kohl appeared to open the door to a solution to the standoff.
In the meantime, the future configuration of the French government could take its toll on markets, analysts said.
"In the coming days the market can move a lot depending on the form of the French government," said Hernansanz.

The Franco-German summit in Poitiers, western France on June 13, and the EU Amsterdam conference in June 16 and 17 will be seen as key appointments for the markets, hunting for suggestions over the shape and the timetable of the forthcoming euro.
And with only a few months before final decision over EMU, dealers added even moderate winds against the union would scare European financial markets, and Spanish ones too.
-- Madrid Newsroom, + 341 585 8340
